rows: A red fox's pupil narrows in bright light to a tall, thin oval, close to a house cat's slit, and its lens has zones that bring several colours into focus together. Out-of-focus things smear up and down in this view.
A red fox sees most sharply in a small central spot, with a weaker band along the horizon. The Arctic fox, which lives on open tundra, has a stronger band.
Red foxes, Arctic foxes and island gray foxes have the same two kinds of colour-sensing cells as dogs. This view shows colours the way a person with red-green colour blindness sees them.
A red fox's retina holds more rods for each cone than an Arctic fox's, the mark of an eye built for night in woodland. This view brightens the shadows.
Maps of the nerve cells in a red fox's retina suggest that it sees about a tenth as much detail as a person. This view is blurred to match.

Red foxes hunting mice pounce mostly toward the north-east, and the pounces that succeed cluster toward the north. With &draw=tide and the motion sensors on, a faint shade follows magnetic north. Whether foxes sense the field is unknown, and the drawing is the app's.
The weights of the centre and the band, the depth of focus, the brightening, the colour's strength and the fall of sharpness from the centre are the app's.
A red fox hears sounds from about 51 to 48,000 vibrations a second, and at 4,000 a second its hearing is keener than a house cat's. This view leaves sound out.
